The Cyton board records 8 E E G channels. Add the Daisy module on top, and you get 8 more: channels 9 to 16. Let's use the 3D model to see how those extra channels get in, and how the two boards stay perfectly in sync.

Each board has its own A D S 1299 chip. The Cyton's chip handles channels 1 to 8. The Daisy's chip handles channels 9 to 16. Same chip, same settings: gain of 24, 24-bit numbers, 250 samples every second.

Your 8 extra electrodes plug into the Daisy's own header, which sits right on top of the Cyton's. Each wire gets the same protection as on the Cyton: a T V S diode underneath, a 2.2 kilo-ohm resistor on top, and a 1 nanofarad capacitor underneath. Then it reaches the Daisy's A D S 1299.

The two boards talk through just 8 pins. Power and ground. The three S P I wires: the clock, the data going in, and the data coming out. These are shared by both chips. A reset line. A clock line. And C S 2, the Daisy's very own chip-select.

Now, how do they stay in sync? Trick number one: one clock. The Daisy has no clock of its own. Its clock-select pin is tied to ground. Instead, the Cyton's chip sends out its 2.048 megahertz clock on the C L K pin, and both chips count the very same ticks. 8,192 ticks make one sample, so both chips finish every sample at exactly the same moment.

Trick number two: one start. The P I C 32 pulls both chip-selects low at the same time, and sends a single START command. Both chips hear it at the same instant. Same start, same clock, so their samples line up, forever. A shared reset line restarts them together, too.

Trick number three: one doorbell. The Daisy's data-ready pin isn't even connected. When the Cyton's chip rings data-ready, the P I C 32 knows the Daisy's sample is ready too. It reads 27 bytes from the Cyton using C S 1, then 27 bytes from the Daisy using C S 2, over the same three wires.

The radio can't carry 16 channels, 250 times a second. So the firmware averages each pair of samples, and takes turns: odd packets carry channels 1 to 8, even packets carry channels 9 to 16. Every channel arrives 125 times a second, and the computer stitches them back into 16.

One clock, one start, one doorbell. That's how two separate chips behave like one 16-channel amplifier. One last tip: the reference pin isn't shared between the boards. For one reference across all 16 channels, join the two S R B pins with a Y-splitter cable.
